extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in civil liberties and the ACLU
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive Wikipedia article describing the American Civil Liberties Union: its history, leadership, funding, policy positions, organizational structure, and major litigation and advocacy themes. Intended as an encyclopedic overview rather than step-by-step guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of legal assistance when civil liberties are at risk
rubrics_metrics.description: The ACLU provides legal assistance in cases where it considers civil liberties at risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal support can take the form of direct legal representation or preparation of amicus curiae briefs expressing legal arguments when another law firm is already providing representation. In addition to representing persons and organizations in lawsuits, the ACLU lobbies for policy positions established by its board of directors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense of free speech including unpopular/offensive speech
rubrics_metrics.description: The ACLU has supported free speech, even when the speech is unpopular or offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official policy notes that the ACLU has represented or defended individuals engaged in some truly offensive speech (communists, Nazis, Ku Klux Klan members, accused terrorists, pornographers, anti-LGBTQ activists, and flag burners) because 'the defense of freedom of speech is most necessary when the message is one most people find repulsive.' Examples cited include defenses of the KKK, neo-Nazis, Westboro Baptist Church, and Unite the Right rally participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy positions / issue priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The ACLU engages in legal advocacy on a set of defined policy positions and issue areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2024 annual report and article list core areas: abortion rights and reproductive health, LGBTQ equality (including same-sex marriage and adoption), immigrants' rights, criminal law reform and decarceration, free speech, voting rights, prisoners' rights, opposition to torture and the death penalty, protecting veterans' housing and employment rights, reforming sex offender registries, and supporting gender-affirming treatments for transgender youth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational/legal structure and constraints (501(c)(3) vs 501(c)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: At the national level the ACLU consists of two legal entities: a 501(c)(4) social welfare group (ACLU) and a 501(c)(3) public charity (ACLU Foundation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both are non-profit organizations that engage in civil rights litigation, advocacy, and education. Donations to the 501(c)(3) foundation are tax-deductible, but donations to the 501(c)(4) are not. The 501(c)(4) group can engage in unlimited political advocacy (including lobbying), but the 501(c)(3) foundation cannot. The two organizations share staff and offices and sometimes leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonpartisan avowal and political independence
rubrics_metrics.description: The ACLU avows a nonpartisan stance and has historically supported figures across the political spectrum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes the organization has received criticism from both liberals and conservatives and gives examples of past support for conservative and liberal figures; the nonpartisan claim is an organizational principle but has been the subject of debate and criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding acceptance policy with respect to civil liberties protections
rubrics_metrics.description: The ACLU evaluates donations for contractual language or conditions that might threaten civil liberties and has rejected funds with problematic clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in October 2004, the ACLU rejected $1.5 million from both the Ford Foundation and Rockefeller Foundation because their donation agreements adopted language from the USA PATRIOT Act, including a clause stipulating none of the money would go to 'underwriting terrorism or other unacceptable activities.' The ACLU viewed such clauses as overly broad and ambiguous and a threat to civil liberties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affiliate autonomy and subsidiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Local ACLU affiliates operate autonomously from the national organization, each with its own staff, executive director, board, and budget.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affiliates typically consist of two non-profit corporations (a 501(c)(3) foundation and a 501(c)(4) ACLU), may solicit their own funding, and sometimes receive national subsidies at the national organization's discretion. The distribution and amount of national assistance vary by state; example: Wyoming affiliate received subsidies until national layoffs led to closure of the Wyoming office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation and advocacy tactics (historic and strategic choices)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ACLU's tactics and case-selection approach have evolved and are part of its implicit decision criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically the ACLU focused on amicus briefs and Supreme Court litigation; in the 1960s it shifted emphasis to direct representation of defendants when initially arrested. The organization also decides whether to take cases based on perceived constitutional stakes and strategic considerations, leading at times to internal debates about whether to defend particular groups or causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional-rooted decision making
rubrics_metrics.description: Many ACLU positions and case choices are explicitly rooted in interpretations of the U.S. Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the article include positions tied to the First Amendment (free speech, separation of church and state), the Second Amendment (opposition to a national gun registry while supporting some gun control), due process and criminal procedure (Miranda, Gideon), and incorporation doctrine origins. The constitutional basis often frames policy nuance rather than absolute stances.
